items.prompt: What is the main job of a persuasive letter?

options.why: That is the job of a story.
That is the job of instructions.

options.text: to make the reader agree with you and do something
to list facts about an animal
options.why: That is the job of a report.

hints: Think about the letter Class 4B wrote to Mrs Wulan.
What did Class 4B want Mrs Wulan to do?
To persuade means to get someone to agree.
items.explanation: A persuasive letter tries to make the reader agree with the writer and take action.

items.prompt: Put the parts of a persuasive letter in order.
items: what you would like to happen next
hints: Letters start with the address and the date.
Then comes the greeting.
The sign-off always comes last.
items.explanation: A letter starts with the address, the date and a greeting. Then it says what you want, gives reasons, and ends with a polite request and a sign-off.

items.prompt: Which sentence is the most persuasive?

options.why: This says what you want, but it gives no reason.

options.text: Please could we have ten more minutes of playtime, because exercise helps us concentrate?

options.why: This is a fact, but it does not persuade.
This is an opinion with no reason.

hints: A persuasive sentence asks politely and gives a reason.
Look for a word that introduces a reason.
Which sentence would a head teacher take seriously?
items.explanation: It asks politely and gives a reason with because. Reasons make a request more persuasive.

items.prompt: Sort the features: persuasive letter or report?

items.text: asks the reader to do something
may have a Did you know? box

hints: A persuasive letter tries to change someone's mind.
A report gives information about a topic.
Start with uses subheadings. Would you see them in a letter or in a report?
items.explanation: Persuasive letters give opinions and reasons, and ask for action. Reports give facts, organised with subheadings.

items.prompt: Which phrase helps you add another reason in a persuasive letter?

options.why: This begins a story.
This ends a story.
Suddenly is used in stories for a surprise.

hints: Persuasive letters give more than one reason.
You need a phrase that adds a new reason.
Which phrase could you use after a sentence that starts with Firstly?
items.explanation: Another reason is introduces a new reason. Words like Firstly, Also and Finally do the same job.

items.prompt: In a report about orangutans, which sentence belongs under the subheading Habitat?

options.text: Orangutans live in the rainforests of Borneo and Sumatra.
Orangutans eat mostly fruit, as well as leaves and insects.
options.why: This belongs under a subheading about food.

options.text: Baby orangutans stay with their mothers for many years.
options.why: This belongs under a subheading about young orangutans.
This belongs under a subheading about what they look like.

hints: Habitat means where an animal lives.
Look for a sentence about a place.
Cross out the sentences about food, babies and bodies.
items.explanation: A habitat is where an animal lives. The rainforests of Borneo and Sumatra are where orangutans live.

items.prompt: Write a letter to your head teacher asking for a school vegetable garden. Give reasons to persuade them.
planning: What exactly are you asking for?
What are your reasons? Can you add a fact as evidence?
What might someone say against it, and how will you answer?
How will you end politely?

criteria.label: I said clearly what I am asking for
I gave reasons, with because or a fact as evidence
I answered a reason someone might give against my idea
I set out my letter with an address, date, greeting and sign-off
I used paragraphs
My spelling and punctuation are careful

hints: Start by saying what you want in one clear sentence.
Use Firstly, Secondly and However to organise your ideas.
items.explanation: A persuasive letter is polite, asks for something clearly and backs it up with reasons and evidence.
items.model:
Class 4C
Cempaka Primary School
10 March

Dear Mrs Wulan,

We are writing to ask if our class could start a vegetable garden behind the canteen.

Firstly, a garden would help us learn. We could measure how fast plants grow in maths and study seeds in science. Secondly, the canteen could cook our vegetables, so pupils would eat fresh food.

Some people might say that a garden needs too much work. However, every pupil in our class has agreed to take turns watering the plants before lessons.

Please could we meet you to share our plan?

Yours sincerely,
Class 4C

items.prompt: Write a letter to your town council asking for a safe crossing outside your school.
planning: Why is the road outside your school hard to cross now?
What would a safe crossing change?
What might the council say against it, and how will you answer?

criteria.label: I explained the problem clearly
I gave reasons and a fact as evidence
I answered a reason someone might give against my idea
I used a formal greeting and sign-off
I used paragraphs
My spelling and punctuation are careful

hints: Describe what happens at the road each morning.
If you do not know the reader's name, end with Yours faithfully.
items.explanation: Persuasive letters work best when they describe a real problem, give evidence and suggest a clear solution.
items.model:
Class 4A
Cempaka Primary School
2 May

Dear Councillors,

We are writing to ask you to build a zebra crossing outside our school gate.

Every morning, more than 300 pupils cross the road outside our school. Cars and motorbikes drive past quickly, and it is hard to find a safe gap. Some younger children wait for a long time before they can cross.

A zebra crossing would make drivers stop, so pupils could cross safely. It would also help parents with babies and older people who use the road.

You might think that a crossing costs a lot. However, keeping children safe on their way to school is worth it.

Yours faithfully,
Class 4A

items.prompt: Persuade your class to choose your idea for the end-of-year trip. Write them a letter.
planning: Where do you want to go?
Give at least two reasons, with facts if you can.
Why is your idea better than another idea someone might suggest?

criteria.label: I made my choice clear at the start
I gave at least two strong reasons
I compared my idea fairly with another idea
I ended by asking the reader to do something
I used paragraphs and linking words
My spelling and punctuation are careful

hints: Think about what your classmates would enjoy and learn.
End with a clear request, such as asking them to vote.
items.explanation: Comparing your idea fairly with another one shows you have thought about it, which makes your letter more convincing.
items.model:
Dear Class 4B,

I think our end-of-year trip should be to the science museum in the city.

Firstly, the museum has a planetarium where we can watch the stars on a giant dome. We have just finished our topic on space, so it would help us remember what we learnt. Secondly, there are rooms where we can build circuits and test magnets ourselves.

Some of you want to go to the water park. It would be fun, but it is very crowded in the holidays, and we can go there with our families at any time.

Please vote for the science museum on Friday!

From your friend,
Nadia

items.prompt: Write a report about an animal that lives in Indonesia. Use a title and subheadings.
planning: Choose your animal and a title.
Plan three or four subheadings, such as Appearance, Habitat, Food and Young.
Write facts, not opinions, and use the present tense.
Add a Did you know? fact at the end.

criteria.label: I used a title and subheadings
I wrote facts, not opinions
Each section is about one thing
I used the present tense
I chose clear words to describe and explain
My spelling and punctuation are careful

hints: Make a quick list of facts under each subheading first.
Read each sentence and ask: could this be checked?
items.explanation: A good report groups facts under clear subheadings and keeps opinions out.
items.model:
Orangutans

Appearance
Orangutans are large apes with long, reddish-brown hair. Their arms are longer than their legs, which helps them swing through the trees.

Habitat
Orangutans live in the rainforests of Borneo and Sumatra. They spend most of their lives high up in the trees.

Food
They eat mostly fruit, such as figs. They also eat leaves, bark and insects.

Young
A baby orangutan stays with its mother for about seven years. She shows it which foods are safe to eat.

Did you know?
Every night, orangutans build a new nest of leaves to sleep in.

items.prompt: Write a news report about an event at your school. It could be sports day or a class trip.
planning: Write a headline that tells the news in a few words.
In the first paragraph, say who, what, when and where.
Add details in order, and a quote from someone who was there.
End with what will happen next.

criteria.label: I wrote a clear headline
My first paragraph says who, what, when and where
I added details in the order they happened
I included a quote with speech marks
I wrote in the past tense
My spelling and punctuation are careful

hints: Look back at the school garden news report for ideas.
Ask someone who was there what they thought, and quote them.
items.explanation: A news report puts the key facts first, then adds details and quotes from people who were there.
items.model:
Blue Team Wins Sports Day

The Blue Team won Cempaka Primary School's Sports Day on Saturday, beating three other teams on the school field.

The day began with the sack race, which the Red Team won. In the afternoon, the Blue Team took the lead in the relay. Their last runner, Fajar, passed two runners on the final bend.

“I was so tired, but I could hear everyone cheering,” said Fajar after the race.

The head teacher, Mrs Wulan, gave out the cup at four o'clock. Next year, the school hopes to add a tug of war.

items.prompt: Write a report about a food from Indonesia, such as rice, tempeh or coconuts. Use subheadings.
planning: Choose your food and a title.
Plan your subheadings, such as What it is and How it is made.
Use facts and the present tense.
Add a fact box or a Did you know? fact.

criteria.label: I used a title and subheadings
I explained how the food is grown or made, in order
I wrote facts, not opinions
I used the present tense
I used clear, exact words
My spelling and punctuation are careful

hints: Ask an adult at home how the food is made, and take notes.
Use time words like first and then when you explain how it is made.
items.explanation: An explanation inside a report uses time words to show the steps in order.
items.model:
Tempeh

What it is
Tempeh is a food made from soya beans. It comes from Java, and people in Indonesia have eaten it for hundreds of years.

How it is made
First, the beans are soaked, boiled and peeled. Then a special mould is mixed in. After one or two days, the mould grows around the beans and holds them together in a firm cake.

How people eat it
Tempeh can be fried, steamed or added to curries. It is often sliced thinly and fried until it is crispy.

Did you know?
Tempeh is full of protein, which helps your body grow and repair itself.

items.prompt: Which sentence would make a strong opening for a persuasive letter about litter?

options.text: I went to the shop yesterday.
options.why: This has nothing to do with the argument.

options.text: Do you want a clean, safe playground for everyone?
Litter is made of different things.
options.why: This is a plain fact and does not draw the reader in.
It is not about the topic.

hints: A persuasive opening makes the reader want to keep reading.
A question can pull the reader in.
Which sentence is about the topic and speaks to the reader?
items.explanation: A question to the reader gets attention and starts the argument about the playground.

items.prompt: Sort each sentence into a reason with evidence or an opinion only.

items.text: Bikes use no petrol, so they save money.
Thirty children in our class cycle.
A helmet protects your head in a fall.

hints: Evidence gives a number or a reason that can be checked.
An opinion only says that something is good.
Look for the word because or so, or a number.
items.explanation: A strong argument gives facts or reasons. Great, cool and better alone do not prove anything.

items.prompt: Which closing sentence is best for a letter asking the head teacher for a new bin?

options.text: That is all I have to say.
options.why: It does not ask for anything.
This does not link to the request.

options.text: Please say yes to the new bin, and our playground will be clean for everyone.

options.why: It is too short and does not ask for action.

hints: A closing line should ask the reader to act.
It should also repeat the benefit.
Which sentence says what you want?
items.explanation: A good ending asks for what you want and says why it helps.

items.prompt: Put the parts of a persuasive paragraph in a sensible order.
items: Add evidence, such as a fact or number.
Answer a worry the reader might have.
End by asking the reader to act.
hints: Begin with your point of view.
A reason needs evidence after it.
The request comes last.
items.explanation: State your aim, give reasons with evidence, answer a worry, and end with a call to action.

items.prompt: "Join us today. Together we can save the turtles!" Which persuasive technique is used here?

options.why: There is no like or as.
There are no facts in these sentences.
The words do not rhyme.

hints: The writer is telling the reader to do something.
Look at the words Join us today.
Which choice means asking the reader to act?
items.explanation: Join us today tells the reader what to do. This is a call to action.

items.prompt: Choose 3 words that make an argument sound more certain.

options.why: Maybe sounds unsure.
Might sounds unsure.

hints: Strong words sound sure.
Which words sound like a guess?
Cross out the two that show doubt.
items.explanation: Definitely, must and surely sound sure. Maybe and might make a writer sound unsure.

items.prompt: Which is the strongest reason for a longer break at school?

options.why: This gives no reason that will convince others.
This is only a personal feeling.
Holidays are not the same as break time.

options.text: A longer break lets children rest and exercise, so they can concentrate better afterwards.

hints: A strong reason explains a benefit.
Ask what the reader gets from your idea.
Which choice uses the word so to link a cause and a result?
items.explanation: A good reason explains how the idea helps. Resting and exercising helps children concentrate.

items.prompt: Which sentence gives a fact to support the argument that litter harms animals?

options.text: Turtles can mistake plastic bags for jellyfish and swallow them.

options.why: This is a feeling, not evidence.
This is a big claim with no proof.
This is a request, not evidence.

hints: You need a fact, not a feeling.
Which sentence tells you what happens to an animal?
Cross out sentences with think, hate or horrible.
items.explanation: This sentence tells what really happens to turtles. It is a fact that supports the argument.
